one_liner: A 15-line C function running eight xoshiro256++ streams in lockstep for compiler auto-vectorization; ~1.9x scalar xoshiro256++, ~3x PCG64.
what_it_does: A single C function `void xoshiro8x256pp(uint64_t s[4][8], uint64_t* r)` in the gist file xoshiro8x256pp.c. Each call advances eight independent xoshiro256++ states, stored structure-of-arrays as s[word][lane], and writes eight 64-bit outputs to r. Seeding is left to the caller (the gist suggests SplitMix64). It has no jump function, wrapper or tests.
how_it_is_fast: It is Vigna's xoshiro256++-vect-speed.c idea fixed at an unroll of 8. Every step of xoshiro256++ (add, rotl 23, shift 17, four XORs, rotl 45) is a separate loop over 8 lanes, so GCC/Clang at -O3 with AVX2 turn each loop into 256-bit vector ops (two registers per word). There are no intrinsics, so the speedup depends entirely on the compiler vectorizing the loops. Eight independent dependency chains also hide latency.
when_to_use: Bulk filling of uint64 buffers (Monte Carlo, noise, test data) on x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512, or aarch64 NEON, where the compiler can vectorize simple loops
When you want xoshiro256++ quality at roughly twice the scalar rate and can consume randoms in blocks of 8
As a small, readable template to copy into your own code base, after you clear its licensing (see when_not_to_use)
when_not_to_use: Without a license you cannot legally copy it as-is. Vigna's public-domain xoshiro256++-vect-speed.c gives the same technique with clear terms.
One-at-a-time draws: you must buffer 8 outputs, and the gain disappears if each call yields only one value
Builds without -O3 or -march flags that enable vectorization (e.g. -O2 on older GCC, or MSVC): the loops may stay scalar and gain nothing
When you need jump/long-jump to separate the 8 lanes: the gist leaves seeding to the user, and poorly seeded lanes may be correlated
Peak bulk throughput: SHISHUA reports far higher GB/s with explicit SIMD

integration.min_toolchain: C99; needs an auto-vectorizing compiler (GCC/Clang -O3, e.g. -march=native) to get the speedup
integration.platforms: any in principle (portable C); measured only on x86-64 (Intel Core i5-8250U, AVX2)
integration.thread_safety: Reentrant: state is caller-owned; use one s[4][8] per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: produces the same per-lane sequence as scalar xoshiro256++ for each lane's state, but returns 8 values per call through a different signature

gotchas: No license is stated on the gist, so the default copyright applies.
The 8 lanes need 8 distinct, well-mixed seeds (e.g. from SplitMix64, or xoshiro jump() between lanes); seeding is not provided.

The benchmark used skeeto/prng64-shootout, which stores each value into a volatile 512 MB buffer one at a time. That likely caps the measured gain below the generator's raw rate; the shootout's own non-PRNG baseline_simd was 12,078 MB/s on the same page.
Before relying on the speedup, check that the compiler vectorized the loops (e.g. -fopt-info-vec).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Xoshiro256PlusSIMD when you want xoshiro256++ (better low bits than xoshiro256+), 8 lanes and portable C with no intrinsics. Pick SHISHUA for maximum bulk throughput, and Sirius64 or wyrand for scalar one-at-a-time draws.
verified_claims_summary: The gist author added the function to skeeto/prng64-shootout and ran it on an Intel Core i5-8250U (compiler and flags not stated; the shootout Makefile defaults to -O3 -march=native). It reached 4,922 MB/s vs 2,619 MB/s for scalar xoshiro256++ and 1,577 MB/s for PCG64, about 1.9x and 3.1x (derived from page data).
status_note: A one-off gist last active 2020-12-22 with no license, so it is reference only. Vigna's CC0 vect-speed.c gives the same technique under copyable terms.
